chapter: Back in New York: Heard and Dizzy
title: His features with Dizzy: Manteca, Body and Soul and the unreleased Yesterdays
summary: His solos included Oo Bop Sha Bam, Manteca and Body and Soul; Yesterdays was not issued because Charlie Ventura had recorded it for the label.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: So, just getting back to being with Dizzy, what was the first tenor solo that you had with Dizzy, do you remember that?

Ahh, let's see. I think it was "Oo Bop Sha Bam" and then I did "Body and Soul", naturally, and then "Manteca" and then I did "Yesterdays" which John Lewis wrote*, he was in the band too, you know. He went later with the Modern Jazz Quartet. That was my feature in the band, yeah. And of course when "Manteca" came out on R.C.A. Victor that was his biggest hit. That did a lot for Dizzy and it did a lot for me, you know. I had sixteen bars and
*possibly an arrangement; Jerome Kern composed "Yesterdays" in 1933; lyrics by Otto Harbach.

everybody liked it, you know. But I was broken hearted because Dizzy was pushin' and the manager Milt Buckner...Milt Shaw...was pushin for me to do "Yes-terdays", but Charlie Ventura had already done it and they didn't go for it, you know. But that really got to me.
You laid it down, but they didn't issue it...is that it?

No, we didn't do it because Charlie Ventura had recorded it earlier for that label, see? And, ooohhh, they were mad about that one. But I did "Manteca" and then "Body and Soul" and I think it was "Oo Bop Sha Bam", that I did. And, you know, everyone was a soloist in that band, you know, and Joe Wilder, he had sixteen bars and that's all he had, you know what I mean, he was a great trumpet player, and we used to wait for that sixteen bars. I think he did it on "Wouldn't You", yeah. That sixteen bars was so tasty. Yeah.
